California, New York and Illinois sued to block the OCC rule in July 2020, and California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina and the District of Columbia sued to block the FDIC rule in August 2020. OppFi said those challenges were dismissed in 2022, but warned that the regulations could be challenged again in the future. In other words, even the federal rules most favourable to the transfer model remained politically contested. [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm)

Illinois remained an important statutory marker even where OppFi's own filing stopped short of giving a fresh case-status update there. The Predatory Loan Prevention Act, signed in March 2021, imposed a 36 per cent APR cap across a broad range of consumer loans. OppFi's filings repeatedly used states such as Illinois as examples of places where the rates charged on programme loans would be impermissible for a non-bank lender. [Illinois Predatory Loan Prevention Act](https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/publicacts/101/PDF/101-0658.pdf) [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm)

## California: The DFPI Case That Mattered Most

California was the most consequential disclosed case because OppFi quantified the business exposure there. Its 2025 annual report said more than 7 per cent of the finance receivables portfolio at December 31, 2025 related to loans originated in California. The litigation chronology, as OppFi itself gave it in the March 31, 2026 10-Q, was precise: complaint filed March 7, 2022; DFPI cross-complaint filed April 8, 2022; OppFi cross-complaint filed October 17, 2022; DFPI preliminary-injunction motion filed January 30, 2023; the court sustained the DFPI's demurrer with leave to amend on September 26, 2023; OppFi filed its amended cross-complaint on October 26, 2023; and the court denied the DFPI's preliminary-injunction motion on October 30, 2023. [OppFi Q1 2026 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000181850226000056/opfi-20260331.htm)

The important shift came in 2025 and early 2026. OppFi said it filed for summary judgment on September 29, 2025, and that on February 24, 2026 the court issued a tentative statement of decision granting OppFi's motion and dismissing the DFPI's cross-claims under the California Financing Law as amended by AB 539. The court, OppFi said, found that the DFPI had failed to raise a triable issue of material fact that OppFi was the true lender or that FinWise was a sham or dummy lender, and further found no evidence that the loans at issue were usurious at inception. [OppFi Q1 2026 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000181850226000056/opfi-20260331.htm)

The frozen-window status was therefore not "appeal likely within 30 days," as the earlier chapter suggested, but something narrower and more procedural. OppFi said it filed a proposed final statement of decision on March 26, 2026; the DFPI filed objections on April 10, 2026; and OppFi had until May 11, 2026 to respond. The DFPI retained appeal rights, but as of the frozen snapshot the most current primary record was still a post-summary-judgment objections process, not a filed appeal. [OppFi Q1 2026 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000181850226000056/opfi-20260331.htm)

## Washington, D.C.: The Earliest Settlement

The District of Columbia provided the cleanest example of an adverse jurisdiction. In November 2021, the D.C. attorney general announced a settlement requiring OppFi to pay $1.5 million to refund more than 4,000 District consumers, waive more than $640,000 in interest owed by those consumers, and pay $250,000 to the District. The attorney general said OppFi had used a bank-partnership structure to charge District residents rates far above the 24 per cent cap. [D.C. OAG release](https://oag.dc.gov/release/ag-racine-announces-over-2-million-settlement)

OppFi's own 2025 annual report corroborated the business consequence. The filing said an April 2021 lawsuit by the District had led FinWise to stop originating loans in Washington, D.C., and that OppFi had ceased doing business there. The same regulatory chapter of the 10-K used the D.C. outcome as part of the broader argument that adverse enforcement could change where the company operated. [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm)

The D.C. complaint also supplied one of the sharper primary-source descriptions of the underlying customer economics. It alleged that roughly half of OppFi customers refinanced their loans, that the average customer refinanced more than twice, and that 75 per cent of OppFi's pre-tax income from OppLoans customers came from refinancing. Those allegations were made in a consumer-protection context, not an investor-relations one, but they remain one of the clearest primary descriptions of how repeat borrowing underpinned the platform. [D.C. AG complaint](https://oag.dc.gov/sites/default/files/2021-04/OppLoans-Complaint-final.pdf)

## Colorado and Other State-Cap Pressure

Colorado mattered less because OppFi disclosed a live company-specific case there, and more because its 2025 filing treated Colorado as a model other states might copy. The company described a settlement between Colorado regulators and two other bank-partnership programmes that capped APRs to Colorado consumers at 36 per cent and required non-bank partners to maintain Colorado licences. OppFi said such a settlement might offer a model for what regulators considered acceptable, but might also invite other states to impose their own standards through enforcement. [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm)

The 2025 annual report then highlighted the next step in Colorado's policy evolution. It said that in June 2023 Colorado enacted a law opting out of interest-rate preemption for state-chartered banks with respect to instalment loans made in Colorado, that the law was expected to take effect on July 1, 2024, and that a preliminary injunction initially blocked enforcement against certain trade-group members. OppFi also said the Tenth Circuit reversed that preliminary injunction in November 2025, while noting that final implementation remained subject to appeals by the trade groups. The company pointed to Iowa and Puerto Rico as other jurisdictions that had exercised the same opt-out. [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm)

## The Other Case on the Docket: Delaware Stockholder Litigation

Not all of OppFi's material legal exposure was about lending law. The 2025 annual report and the March 2026 quarterly report also disclosed a Delaware Court of Chancery action filed on July 20, 2023 on behalf of a putative class of former FG New America Acquisition Corp. stockholders. The amended complaint, filed February 7, 2025, added Todd Schwartz, Theodore Schwartz, Schwartz Capital Group, OppFi's former chief executive officer and a former investment banker as alleged aiders and abettors of the SPAC-era defendants' fiduciary breaches. OppFi itself was not a party, but the company and OppFi-LLC were obligated to indemnify certain defendants and had tendered the defence to their D&O policies. [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm) [OppFi Q1 2026 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000181850226000056/opfi-20260331.htm)

The status advanced inside the frozen window. The March 31, 2026 10-Q said the parties filed a stipulation of settlement on April 24, 2026 and were awaiting a hearing on the settlement agreement, anticipated for September 2026. The same 10-Q said OppFi carried $13.0 million of estimated legal contingent liabilities and $8.5 million of related insurance recoveries as of both March 31, 2026 and December 31, 2025. [OppFi Q1 2026 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000181850226000056/opfi-20260331.htm)

## OppFi's Strategic Response

By the frozen window, the most consequential strategic response to this legal map was not another courtroom argument. It was the BNCCORP transaction. OppFi's April 28, 2026 8-K paired the proposed BNC National Bank acquisition with a completed corporate simplification that exchanged all retained OppFi units into Class A stock, cancelled the remaining Class V voting stock, and fixed a $40.8 million early-termination payment under the tax receivable agreement. The companion merger agreement set cash-and-stock consideration at $19.375 plus 1.90 OppFi shares for each BNCC share and valued the deal at about $130.7 million based on OppFi's closing price on April 28, 2026. [OppFi BNCC 8-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000030/opfi-20260428.htm)

That pairing mattered because it showed what OppFi thought the regulatory problem actually was. The company could keep litigating the bank-partnership model state by state, and in California it had just won its strongest ruling to date. But the strategic answer it chose inside the frozen window was to buy a national bank, simplify its structure and move toward a regime where the charter sat inside the group rather than outside it. The litigation map was still the business map. OppFi had simply decided to redraw it rather than defend the old one indefinitely. [OppFi BNCC 8-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000030/opfi-20260428.htm)

chapters.title: Timeline from 2012 founding through SPAC listing and litigation milestones
chapters.body:
## From Kitchen Table to Capital Markets: The Founding Proposition

Schwartz launched Opportunity Financial in 2012 with a thesis that non-prime borrowers — salaried Americans with FICO scores below 650 — were underserved, not uncreditworthy. The bank-partnership model built around that thesis leveraged federal rate-exportation authority to serve borrowers nationally while avoiding state-by-state licensing constraints.

## The SPAC Pivot and the NYSE Listing

OppFi completed its combination with FG New America Acquisition Corp. in July 2021, listing on NYSE under the up-C structure common to founder-led fintech SPACs. The timing proved, in retrospect, almost precisely wrong — the listing arrived at a late-cycle moment just before the credit environment inflected adversely.

## True-Lender Litigation: The Long Reckoning

State attorneys general and regulators assembled true-lender challenges across California, Colorado, New York, and the District of Columbia — each adverse outcome compressing addressable market directly. (See *Litigation & Regulatory* chapter for detailed coverage.)

## The Credit-Cycle Trough: 2022–2023

Simultaneous with litigation, OppFi navigated the most difficult credit environment for non-prime lending in more than a decade. The 2022–2023 vintages experienced elevated charge-offs; SalaryTap was paused. (See *Earnings Story* and *Financial Deep Dive* for detailed coverage.)

## The 2024 Recovery

By fiscal 2024, tighter-underwritten cohorts were producing normalized charge-offs and sustainably positive profitability.

## Forward Catalysts

Three dynamics define OppFi's forward trajectory: (1) the litigation pipeline — binary events capable of adding or removing hundreds of millions of addressable origination volume; (2) multi-product expansion via the OppFi Card; and (3) the consumer-credit cycle. Whether the true-lender litigation crucible produces durable legal clarity or continued jurisdictional attrition remains the central unresolved question.

chapters.title: Litigation, credit cycle, funding, governance, regulatory, competitive risks
chapters.body:
## The True-Lender Crucible

The most existential risk OppFi carried into 2026 was true-lender litigation — the contested proposition that its bank partners, not OppFi, are the lenders entitled to federal rate preemption. Where that proposition fails, OppFi's product becomes unlawful. California, Colorado, Washington, D.C., and Illinois each pursued enforcement actions (see *Litigation & Regulatory* chapter for detailed coverage).

Each adverse outcome compressed OppFi's geographic addressable market in a compounding manner. As [OppFi 10-K filings on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=OPFI&type=10-K) documented, the company was required to include growing state-by-state disclosure of jurisdictions where it had curtailed or ceased originating loans. By late 2024, the map of inactive or legally contested geographies included several of the most populous US states. Management characterised the situation as a litigation portfolio rather than a regulatory posture — each case individuated, each appealable — but the cumulative effect was that the total-addressable-market number embedded in investor presentations quietly narrowed. The structural asymmetry was punishing: an adverse ruling cost OppFi a state permanently (or until the law changed) while a favourable ruling merely confirmed ground it already held.

## Charge-Off Volatility and the Cycle Scar

The 2022–2023 vintages left a deep scar: elevated charge-offs, swings from profitability to net loss, and origination compression. The 2024 recovery proved the underwriting tightening worked, but demonstrated how quickly non-prime performance can deteriorate. A second credit dislocation would restart the cycle.

## Warehouse Risk and Rate Sensitivity

OppFi's funding model amplified both the credit-cycle and rate risks. The company funded its purchase of receivables from bank partners primarily through revolving warehouse credit facilities extended by major bank lenders. Those facilities carried floating-rate pricing, renewing periodically under negotiated terms. The combination of floating-rate cost of funds against a portfolio of fixed-rate consumer loans created structural margin compression whenever short-term rates rose, precisely the condition that prevailed through 2022 and 2023 as the Federal Reserve's tightening cycle pushed SOFR above five percent.

Facility renewal risk compounded the interest-rate exposure. Warehouse lenders reassess counterparty credit quality at renewal, and a platform lender reporting elevated charge-offs and net losses — as OppFi was during the 2022-2023 trough — presents a less attractive borrower than in calmer conditions. The concentration of funding across a limited number of bank facilities meant that a single lender's withdrawal or material tightening of advance-rate terms could force a reduction in origination capacity with little warning. The company disclosed these risks in standard 10-K fashion, but the qualitative language understated the operational reality: warehouse availability was a binding constraint on growth, and its terms moved inversely with OppFi's credit quality.

## Governance: The Up-C Overhang

The up-C structure (detailed in *Business Model*) created governance complexity: Todd Schwartz retained effective voting control through Class B shares, insulating management from market discipline. The TRA transferred economic value from public shareholders to insiders at each exchange event, reinforcing the structural subordination of public minority shareholders.

## Federal Regulatory Exposure and CFPB Dynamics

The federal regulatory landscape shifted meaningfully with the change of administration in January 2025. The CFPB under the Biden administration had been an active antagonist of high-rate bank-partnership lending, pursuing rulemaking on small-dollar credit and publishing interpretive guidance that questioned the scope of federal preemption for fintech-bank arrangements. The Trump administration's move to curtail CFPB enforcement activity in early 2025 reduced the near-term federal regulatory pressure on OppFi's model, but it did not eliminate it — the Bureau's enabling statute remained intact, appropriations litigation notwithstanding, and a future administration could reconstitute its enforcement posture. Congressional Democrats continued to advance versions of the Veterans and Consumers Fair Credit Act, which would impose a 36% APR cap federally across all consumer credit including bank-originated loans, effectively prohibiting OppFi's product nationally. The bill had not passed as of the frozen window, but its periodic reintroduction served as a standing reminder that the regulatory floor beneath the bank-partnership model was political as much as legal.

## Competitive Pressure

Enova and OneMain operate at larger scale with structural advantages (Enova's diversification; OneMain's direct-licensing model without true-lender exposure). BNPL platforms add margin pressure on customer acquisition cost. (See *Competitive Position* chapter for detailed analysis.)

Together, the six risk vectors — state-level litigation, credit-cycle volatility, warehouse funding fragility, governance structure, federal regulatory exposure, and competitive intensity — constituted a risk profile unusual even within the non-prime category.

chapters.title: Litigation resolution paths, multi-product expansion, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The fork in the road: litigation and the charter question

By the frozen window, OppFi's strategic horizon had narrowed to two connected variables rather than one. The first was whether the California true-lender win would survive objections and any appeal. The second was whether the BNCCORP acquisition would close on the timetable management outlined. The business no longer needed a speculative product roadmap to explain its next phase; it needed legal durability for the existing model or a successful migration into a chartered one. [OppFi Q1 2026 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000181850226000056/opfi-20260331.htm) [OppFi BNCC 8-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000030/opfi-20260428.htm)

## Path A: the bank-partner model survives, but geography stays political

In the first path, OppFi would keep winning enough of the legal arguments around rate exportation and true-lender status to preserve a viable multi-state footprint for OppLoans. The company entered 2026 from a position of operating strength. In March 2026 it guided to full-year 2026 revenue of $650 million to $675 million, adjusted net income of $153 million to $160 million and adjusted EPS of $1.76 to $1.84. Those numbers assumed the lending engine could keep compounding without an immediate legal shock. [OppFi FY2025 earnings release](https://investors.oppfi.com/news/news-details/2026/OppFi-Reports-Record-Annual-Revenue-Net-Income-and-Adjusted-Net-Income/default.aspx)

But even in that more favourable path, the map would stay political. OppFi's 2025 annual report said more than 7 per cent of year-end receivables were tied to California, and the same filing treated state opt-outs and state-cap statutes as active threats to future growth. Survival under the bank-partner model would therefore not mean the litigation years were over; it would mean they had become a permanent cost of doing business. [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm)

## Path B: the charter closes and the model changes shape

The second path was the one management itself chose to pursue. OppFi's April 2026 8-K said the BNCCORP transaction was expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to BNCC shareholder approval and approvals from the OCC and the Federal Reserve. The company said existing OppFi holders were expected to own about 93 per cent of the combined company and former BNCC holders about 7 per cent. If that deal closed, the key regulatory fact about OppFi would no longer be that it partnered with banks; it would be that it owned one. [OppFi BNCC 8-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000030/opfi-20260428.htm)

That path also made the older OppFi Card hedge thesis obsolete. By the frozen window, OppFi was not taking new applications for OppFi Card or SalaryTap, and had already completed the OppFi Card wind-down in January 2024. The live diversification bet was the charter itself, plus adjacent assets such as Bitty, not a return to the paused consumer products once described as a broader suite. [OppFi 2024 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850225000003/opfi-20241231.htm) [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm)

## Consumer-credit cycle: repaired, not conquered

The operating numbers suggested OppFi had earned the right to plan, but not to relax. The March 31, 2026 10-Q said average yield in the first quarter slipped to 130.7 per cent from 135.8 per cent a year earlier because more delinquent loans were not accruing interest. Total net originations for the quarter fell to $176.0 million from $189.2 million a year earlier, even as funding capacity improved to about $624.9 million. In other words, the company had more room on the balance sheet than it had in 2022, but it was still navigating a borrower base whose performance could soften quickly. [OppFi Q1 2026 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001818502/000181850226000056/opfi-20260331.htm)

## The 2026-2030 posture

The cleanest way to state the outlook by May 23, 2026 was this: OppFi had already proved that the core instalment platform could be highly profitable if loss rates stayed in the high-30s to high-40s rather than the low-60s. What it had not yet proved was whether that earnings power belonged to a durable national franchise or to a legally contingent one. The company responded by simplifying the Up-C, terminating the tax receivable structure for $40.8 million, and trying to bring the charter inside the walls. Whether that move ultimately reduced regulatory risk or merely relocated it from state courts to bank supervision was the question that would define the next chapter. [OppFi 2025 10-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000019/opfi-20251231.htm) [OppFi BNCC 8-K, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1818502/000181850226000030/opfi-20260428.htm)

**Products:**

## Competitive Set

| Peer | Model | Primary Product |
|------|-------|----------------|
| Enova International | Direct lender + marketplace | Personal loans, SMB lending |
| Curo Group | Direct lender, storefront + online | Payday, installment |
| OneMain Financial | Direct lender | Personal installment loans |
| Elevate Credit | Bank-partnership model | Rise installment, Elastic line of credit |
| World Acceptance Corp. | Direct lender, branch network | Small personal loans |

OppFi's differentiator within this set was its pure-platform posture — marketing, technology, and servicing layered atop FDIC-insured bank partners — which enabled rate exportation under federal preemption but simultaneously concentrated regulatory exposure in the true-lender doctrine.

---

## True-Lender Litigation Status (as of 2026-05-23)

| Jurisdiction | Nature of Challenge | Status |
|--------------|---------------------|--------|
| California | State AG / plaintiff bar: OppFi is the true lender; subject to CA usury caps | Ongoing / contested |
| Colorado | State usury-cap enforcement challenge to bank-partnership model | Ongoing |
| Washington D.C. | District AG action against rent-a-bank arrangements | Ongoing |
| New York | Consumer protection and usury challenges | Ongoing |

Each adverse resolution compresses the addressable non-prime consumer market; each favorable outcome preserves or expands it. This binary litigation pipeline defined OppFi's strategic posture through the 2024–2026 period.

---

## Corporate Structure Reference

OppFi operates as an **Up-C** holding company. Class A shares trade on NYSE as OPFI; Class B shares remain with founder-related entities. Operating-LLC units held by Class B shareholders are exchangeable into Class A shares. Tax distributions to LLC unit holders are a recurring cash obligation under the structure.
